videos.title: Alcohol Oxidation Practical: Identifying the Products | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Alcohol Oxidation Practical: Identifying the Products | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson12.sa.html

Acidified dichromate turns green when an alcohol is oxidised, but which product did you make? Investigate the oxidation of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol: sort alcohols with a water-bath test and a control, distil off an aldehyde, reflux to an acid, and test each distillate with Tollens' reagent, Benedict's solution and litmus. See why you test the distillate, not the flask, how known samples make results trustworthy, and how to handle and dispose of chromium(VI), silver and organic residues safely. Green says oxidised; the test says what. Two practice questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

"describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisites: Where can an alcohol reaction lead? Aldehydes and ketones. Next: Why are carboxylic acids acidic?

videos.title: Making an Ester: Esterification Practical and Percentage Yield | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Making an Ester: Esterification Practical and Percentage Yield | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson15.sa.html

A class makes pentyl ethanoate, the banana-smelling ester, and gets about 60% of the most it could make. Is that a failed practical? Prepare an ester under reflux safely, get it out with a separating funnel, calculate the percentage yield from the limiting reactant, and see why equilibrium sets a ceiling while losses take the yield lower. Test whether excess ethanoic acid raises the yield, judge the results for reliability, accuracy and validity, and learn the safe handling and disposal of concentrated sulfuric acid and flammable organics. Two practice questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

videos.title: Soap vs Detergent in Hard Water: Practical Investigation | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Soap vs Detergent in Hard Water: Practical Investigation | Year 12 Chemistry Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson17.sa.html

In soft water, soap and detergent both froth. In hard water, soap turns cloudy and barely froths, while the detergent keeps working. Set up a fair comparison with hard water made from calcium chloride, matched tubes and controls; measure froth height and how long oil stays emulsified; and use the results to explain scum formation, soap-coated oil droplets and why a detergent's head group survives hard water. Judge the results for validity, reliability and accuracy, and handle and dispose of the chemicals safely. Soap makes scum in hard water; detergents mostly don't. Two practice questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

A PET bottle and a nylon rope are both built by joining small molecules that lose a water molecule at every link. See why condensation monomers need a reactive group at each end, how PET (a polyester) and nylon 6,6 (a polyamide) form, how to draw a repeat unit and get the monomers back by adding the water back, how condensation compares with addition polymerisation, and why hydrogen bonds make nylon tough while stiff rings make PET strong. videos.title: Antibiotic Disc Practical: Zones of Inhibition and What They Show | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Antibiotic Disc Practical: Zones of Inhibition and What They Show | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson16.sa.html

Three antibiotic discs on one plate: one clears a 25 mm zone, one a 15 mm zone, one nothing. Does the biggest zone mean the best medicine? Learn why a zone of inhibition forms, how to run a safe, fair disc test (a lawn of an approved harmless culture, spaced discs, a blank control, three plates, kept closed at 25 to 30 °C and never opened), and how to measure zones through the base. Then see what zone size depends on, why a plate isn't a patient, and how to judge validity, reliability and accuracy. Includes a risk assessment and two exam-style questions with brief feedback. All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

- antivirals

Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisites: Why do antibiotics and antivirals work differently? and Microbial testing of water or food. Next: How can vector control reduce infection?

Graph questions lose marks on the mechanics: uneven scales, missing units, dot-to-dot lines, and trends described without numbers. Learn to read the axes first, draw a graph that earns its marks (TAILS, then a line or curve of best fit), describe a trend with direction, data and any change, read a value between points, and judge a prediction made beyond the data. See a worked Biology question on antibiotic resistance data, then try two training questions, one in Chemistry (fix a student's graph) and one in Biology (describe a relationship). All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

"derive trends, patterns and relationships in data and information"

videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson01.sa.html

Chloride can't be seen, and it isn't an acid or a base, so how does a titration find it? See how silver nitrate turns chloride into white silver chloride, why a little potassium chromate gives a red-brown endpoint only once the chloride is nearly gone, and why that order comes from the silver each solid needs, not from which salt is less soluble. Learn the pH window and what acid does to the titre, then turn concordant titres into a chloride concentration in mol/L and g/L. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.originalTitle: Gravimetric Analysis: From Precipitate Mass to Ion Concentration | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson02.sa.html

A clear wastewater sample turns cloudy white when barium ions are added, and the mass of that dried solid tells you how much sulfate was there. See why barium sulfate is chosen over calcium sulfate using Ksp, why the precipitate is digested, washed and dried to constant mass, and how to turn a mass found by difference into a percentage and a concentration. Then learn which errors make the answer too high or too low, and why repeating an analysis doesn't fix them. Two exam-style questions at the end.

Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):

- gravimetric analysis

videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson01.sa.html

You lose heat to the room around you every second, yet your core temperature stays close to 37 °C. Learn what homeostasis means, why body conditions are held within a tolerance range around a set point, and how the five parts of a feedback loop (stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector and response) correct a change. See why the loop is called negative feedback, why the extra response eases as conditions recover, and how positive feedback differs. Then practise constructing a loop from a description and interpreting a temperature graph.

On a hot day you pass a little dark urine; after a litre of water you pass a lot of pale urine. Learn why the variable your body regulates is blood concentration (osmolarity), how your kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and take most of it back, how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary, and how ADH puts water channels (aquaporins) into the collecting ducts. See the same negative feedback loop run in reverse after drinking water, and how aldosterone differs: water follows salt. Then practise predicting urine after a salty snack and interpreting a urine output graph.
